summary: Flame in Freefall (Kestrel IV) is a browser game that teaches how flames behave in microgravity and how far to trust a model. Players read real conditions from NASA ISS combustion experiments, guess whether the flame keeps burning or goes out, then ignite it. The game reveals our model's odds, its uncertainty, and the three closest real experiments, labelled as recorded, derived or estimated. The models are trained on three NASA ISS data sets and run entirely in the browser. It matters because spacecraft fire safety depends on understanding microgravity combustion, and because people should learn to read uncertainty, not just answers.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: Quick play is a 10-round guessing game built from real ISS experiment conditions. After each guess it shows the model's call, probability, uncertainty, a simulated flame, and the three nearest real experiments. Lab mode adds a level map, missions, sliders and upgrades. Raya, a fictional scientist, guides new players.

HOW IT WORKS: I cleaned three NASA PSI data sets (PSI-159, PSI-39, PSI-69) and trained and calibrated classifiers with grouped cross-validation. Uncertainty comes from a bootstrap ensemble and distance to real experiments. Models are exported as JSON and scored in the browser. No server, no live model calls.

BENEFIT AND IMPACT: Builds intuition for microgravity flames and for telling recorded, derived and modelled evidence apart.

CREATIVE: A pixel-art space RPG wrapper around honest science, with limits always visible: estimates come from a few hundred ISS experiments and are not predictions for the Moon, Mars or any other gravity. Ship, crew and planets are labelled fiction.

TOOLS: JavaScript, WebGL2, HTML/CSS, Python (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Pillow), Playwright, Cloudflare Workers.

SI USE: Code, tests and docs were written with AI assistants (Claude, Codex, DeepSeek) directed by the team, who made the design decisions. Pixel art and background music were generated by code.
